strengths: The specifically tailored development of machine learning methods for crystal structures is an important problem with relevance for the society. Because of this also machine learning conferences like ICLR should be open for publications that develop these specific methods.
Modeling the periodic molecules is an important subject for material discovery.
The experiments are fairly conducted on a common benchmark for materials.
Numerical results seem moderately impressive and the authors seem knowledgeable about GNNs / Transformers in the context of crystallography.

Crystal materials property prediction is a complicated natural science task. I think the authors did a good job on delineating and explaining the concepts of this task, and break down into smaller modules easier to understand.

In section 3.3, while I think the contents are organized well by explaining the architecture of each sub-module one by one, it would be better to further explain the motivations behind each sub-module, since the proposed system is large and complicated.
The authors did a quite thorough analysis on model depth and other hyper-params, on up to 8 datasets, comparing against 6 baselines. The results look promising and convincing.
weaknesses: The positional encoding is not E(3) invariant or equivariant, thus unsuitable for modeling the properties of materials.
Cartesian coordinates are extrinsic; using them directly is not equivariant to E(3) transformations, which may hinder generalization to rotated crystal structures.
Fractional coordinates are also extrinsic and suffer the same issues as Cartesian coordinates, making them unsuitable for creating E(3) invariant representations.

Laplace embedding and Random walk encoding are redundant terminology-wise; while intrinsic, they do not capture the full 3D geometry of the crystal, and a combination of intrinsic and extrinsic features is necessary with extrinsic features needing E(3) invariance or equivariance.

Multi Head Neighbor Attention appears to be just normal multi head attention on the line graph and should be stated as such, not presented as a new method; the description does not clearly distinguish it from standard multi-head attention mechanisms applied to a graph.
The phrase "holistic representation of spatial information" is awkward terminology; the representation should be described in terms of E(3) equivariance rather than using "holistic".

It is not described why modeling the long-range interaction is the key to modeling the periodic molecules; the tackled GNN's limitation is a general problem in the graph field and does not need to be restricted to modeling periodic structures.

From the results of Figure 5 and 6, the effectiveness of modeling the long-range interaction by using the transformer seems insignificant; performance gains from adding the graph-wise transformer (GwT) are marginal, especially when the number of eTGC layers is increased, suggesting the model may not effectively leverage long-range interactions.

Even though the proposed method leverages transformers which require more memory space, the performances are not significant compared to the baselines; the computational overhead of the transformer architecture does not seem to be justified by the performance gains, and a more detailed analysis of computational cost and memory usage is needed.

It is not explained what the tasks are; abbreviations for material properties are not defined, making it difficult to understand the specific prediction goals; the authors should clearly state what material properties are being predicted and provide context for why these properties are important.
Method seems only slightly different than existing approaches (essentially being a linear combination of existing methods) and only achieves moderately good numerical results.
There are numerous typos and grammar / spelling errors.

In section 3.1.3, $u'$ and $v'$ are unclear whether they represent edges or abstract angles; a more precise definition relating these symbols to the crystal structure and $t_{ijk}$ notation is needed.

The rationale for using multiple positional encodings is not fully explained; it is unclear how each encoding contributes to performance and whether some are redundant, and ablation studies would be helpful.
The related work section should be expanded to include recent advances in crystal materials property prediction, especially those employing GNNs and contrastive learning techniques (e.g., [1, 2]).
A running example (e.g., one simple crystal structure) would help explain how each module and inputs/outputs are connected; a step-by-step walkthrough would improve understanding.
